claims.statement: After the elemental diet, reintroduce foods in four progressive phases: Phase 1 = easiest-to-digest foods (cooked, pureed vegetables, bone broth, well-cooked fruits); Phase 4 = common allergens (wheat, dairy, corn, potatoes). Test one new food per day (or one every 3 days for rigorous testing). At the end of each week, stay on just those 7 foods for another week to confirm.
claims.evidence_excerpt: One clinical trial on food reintroduction triggers. Thompson's personal experience and reader feedback. The phase structure is based on general digestibility principles.

claims.statement: Dr. Arthur Coca's pulse test (1950s): take pulse before eating, then 3 times at 30-minute intervals after eating a single food. If pulse increases beyond normal range (typically >16 BPM variation), food allergy is suspected. Thompson includes the full procedure and claims the test detected triggers for conditions including colitis, GI bleeding, abdominal pain, and many others.
claims.evidence_excerpt: Coca's clinical observations from the 1950s. No modern validation. Thompson acknowledges limitations: not effective for hay fever, asthma, eczema, or contact dermatitis; invalidated by caffeine, smoking, or beta-blockers.

claims.statement: I began to notice other unanticipated benefits. Patients with muscle aches, stiff joints, and even full-blown arthritis, chronic skin rashes, psoriasis, generalized fatigue and 'spaciness' were alleviated. Elaine Gottschall's diet had probably reduced intestinal toxicity.
claims.evidence_excerpt: Clinical observation only. No controlled data, no systematic tracking.

Alternative practitioners try to replace antibiotics with natural antimicrobial substances, essentially following the same idea. But the key is to improve stomach acid production and provide healing for the gut lining.

claims.statement: One of the best ways to fight inflammation is to adopt an anti-inflammatory diet.
claims.evidence_excerpt: General nutritional science consensus. No specific trials cited for this food list. The anti-inflammatory framing draws on Mediterranean diet research and individual food component studies (curcumin in turmeric, omega-3s in fatty fish, polyphenols in berries).

claims.statement: One oversimplification Elaine Gottschall's book avoids is the notion that food allergy is the source of many gastrointestinal complaints... The more sophisticated belief that it is not individual foods themselves but the byproducts of ingestion of certain foods that cause intestinal problems is fast replacing the concept of food allergy.
claims.evidence_excerpt: Hoffman references Dr. J.O. Hunter's 1991 Lancet article (not directly cited, but referenced as "landmark") and "another recent Lancet article" on intolerances to corn, wheat, milk, potatoes, and rye.

claims.statement: Space your meals four to five hours apart. You want to give your stomach time to empty and your migrating motor complex a chance to sweep out whatever is left in your small intestine after digestion before you send more down the tube.
claims.evidence_excerpt: This is Pimentel's MMC theory, presented without citation in Sarna's voice.

claims.statement: Some starchy foods which were assumed to be digested completely are, in fact, incompletely digested by most people. In those people with intestinal disorders, the digestibility of starch is even further affected.
claims.evidence_excerpt: References to incomplete starch digestion in healthy people, genetic variation in starch types (rice, corn strains), and the amylose/amylopectin distinction. Notes that some intestinal bacteria are "made more virulent by the presence of undigested cornstarch in the intestine."
